clue.text: Escape, say, into the world of books?

indicators.note: into tells us the abbreviation for 'say' is placed within the word for literature

parts.note: the world of books is literature, shortened to LIT
say, as in 'for example', is abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether reading is a form of escapism into a world of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Escape, say' reads as escapism by example, but 'say' gives EG, which goes 'into' LIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To leg it is British slang for to run away, a lively synonym of flee.

clue.text: Roasted meat eaten after starter's polished off

parts.note: lamb is a meat

indicators.note: starter's polished off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: tasted is used loosely for eaten, sampled

explanation.surface: Lamb was roasted and eaten once the first course had been finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roasted' looks like cooking but means severely criticised; 'starter' is the first letter, not a first course.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast someone is to criticise them harshly, and to lambast is to berate fiercely.

clue.text: Greek pledge only half kept after a power struggle

indicators.note: after means the half of pledge follows the other pieces

parts.note: P is the physics abbreviation for power

indicators.note: only half kept means just the first three of the six letters remain

explanation.surface: A Greek promise only half honoured after a struggle for power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only half kept' keeps the first three of pledge's six letters; 'after' places that half at the end, though the clue mentions it before 'a power'.
explanation.definitionFit: To grapple is to wrestle or tussle with someone.

clue.text: Boozer closed? Traveller is upset

parts.note: a door pushed to is closed, so to means shut

indicators.note: is upset means the traveller's word is turned over, read backwards in this down clue

parts.note: a rep, a sales representative, is a commercial traveller

explanation.surface: A traveller is upset to find the pub shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, but here a heavy drinker; 'is upset' turns REP to PER.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is a habitual drinker, an old word for a drunkard.

clue.text: Defeat hard to take in public dispute

indicators.note: to take in means the words for public and dispute together enclose the letter for hard

parts.note: public, as in open and not hidden, is overt
a dispute is a row, a noisy quarrel
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A loss is hard to accept when it ends in a public quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take in' sounds like accepting a defeat, but it means the two words for public and dispute enclose the letter for hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Overthrowing a ruler means toppling or vanquishing them, so it is a synonym of beat in battle.

clue.text: Coat perhaps (but not hat) fellow needed to protect part of body?

definitions.text: Coat perhaps (but not hat) fellow needed to protect part of body?

indicators.note: but not hat means the word loses its top, its first letter, like a head without its hat

parts.note: to coat something is, for example, to cover it

indicators.note: needed to protect means the fellow's word wraps around the body part's word

parts.note: a gent is a fellow, a man
the arm is a part of the body

explanation.surface: Someone describes a coat, as opposed to a hat, that a man wears to shield his body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hat' is the top of a word, so 'but not hat' beheads the word for coat. The whole clue also describes the answer: a coat, not headwear, that protects the body.
explanation.definitionFit: An outer layer such as a coat or cloak is worn on top of other clothes.

clue.text: Small creature written about in Beowulf legend

indicators.note: written about means the letters are turned round, read backwards
in means the letters sit inside the run of the clue words

explanation.surface: A tiny being appears in the Old English epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written about' turns FLE, hidden 'in' BeowulF LEgend, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Elves are small mythical beings of folklore.

clue.text: Work that tires Oscar winner

indicators.note: work means the letters of the next two words are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone finds that toil exhausts even an Academy Award winner.
explanation.walkthrough: The Artist, a silent black-and-white film, won the Best Picture Oscar for 2011.
explanation.definitionFit: The Artist took the top Academy Award for best film.

clue.text: He composed Supremes singer's popular No 1

parts.note: Diana Ross was the lead singer of the Supremes
in means popular, fashionable
number one is I as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A composer had the Supremes' singer's big hit.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan gives 'No!', but the wordplay needs No 1 (Roman I). 'He composed' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini was the Italian opera composer of The Barber of Seville.

clue.text: Writing off pounds corrupt lawyer spent

indicators.note: corrupt means the remaining letters are spoiled into a new order
writing off means the letter for pounds is cancelled from the word lawyer

parts.note: L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pounds sterling

explanation.surface: A crooked lawyer has his fees written off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writing off' removes L from LAWYER, leaving AWYER, which 'corrupt' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Spent here means exhausted, worn out, tired.

clue.text: Politician about to consume crusts of imaginative pastry dish

indicators.note: about means the politician's letters go around the verb for consuming

parts.note: MP, Member of Parliament, is the standard abbreviation for a politician
to consume food is to eat it

indicators.note: crusts are the outer edges, so take the first and last letters of the next word

explanation.surface: An MP is about to tuck into an inventive pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reads as 'on the point of', but it is the container signal; 'crusts of' means the outer letters of imaginative.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie filled with minced or chunked flesh is a savoury baked pastry dish.

clue.text: It's said cold snap's the reverse of ideal for a tender plant

indicators.note: it's said means the word for a cold snap is heard rather than read

parts.note: a cold snap brings a freeze

indicators.note: the reverse of means the term for ideal is read backwards

parts.note: A1 (written AI, A-one) means first-rate or ideal

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that a sudden frost is the worst thing for a delicate bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's said' makes FREEZE heard as FREES; 'the reverse of' turns A1 (A-one, first-class, here AI) into IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Freesias are fragrant flowering bulbs from South Africa, not frost-hardy, so gardeners treat them as tender.

clue.text: A health club rejected dear vegetable

parts.note: a health club is a spa

indicators.note: rejected means the endearment is sent back, read in reverse

parts.note: sugar is a term of endearment, like dear or honey

explanation.surface: Someone turns down an expensive vegetable at the gym's café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dear' looks like 'expensive' but is the endearment SUGAR; 'rejected' turns it into RAGUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Asparagus spears are green shoots eaten as a seasonal vegetable.

clue.text: Machine responsible for weight loss?

parts.note: a stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds, so something that cuts stones causes a loss of weight, though really it shapes rock

explanation.definitionFit: A tool or worker that cuts and dresses rock; a stone is a British unit of weight, hence the dieting joke.

clue.text: After short storm, New York's very wet

indicators.note: short means the word for storm loses its last letter

parts.note: to storm a place is to raid it
NY is the standard abbreviation for New York

explanation.surface: After a brief downpour New York is soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storm' looks like weather but is the verb, an attack: RAID, cut to RAI by 'short'.
explanation.definitionFit: A day with lots of precipitation is wet weather, so a showery climate is a damp one.

clue.text: Attire regularly features this?

indicators.note: regularly means take every other letter of the word attire, here the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: A dress code often includes a certain neckwear item.
explanation.walkthrough: Every other letter of ATTIRE, starting with the second, gives the answer, and the whole clue also says formal clothing often includes one.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is a common feature of formal clothing, worn with a shirt and suit.

clue.text: They're unusual dishes into which port is tipped

indicators.note: into which means the following letters go inside the word for dishes

parts.note: dishes is slang for attractive people, cuties
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port, shortened to Rio

indicators.note: tipped means the little word is turned over, read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone describes odd dishes over which a fortified wine has been poured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dishes' suggests food and 'port' wine, but dishes are attractive people; 'into which' sends the port and the 'tipped' little word inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Curios are odd collectables, so strange things are rarities or oddities.

clue.text: Letter concerning family member written in jargon

indicators.note: written in means the two words are placed inside the word for jargon

parts.note: cant is jargon, the special talk of a group
on means about or concerning
a son is a family member

explanation.surface: A letter about a relative is written in technical language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like correspondence but is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Consonants are alphabet characters other than the vowels, such as B or T.

clue.text: Band in small marquee, demanding …

indicators.note: in means the band's word goes inside the marquee's word

parts.note: a marquee is a large tent
a ring is a band, as worn on a finger

explanation.surface: A band playing in a little marquee is making demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests musicians but is a RING.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringent rules are strict, exacting, severe.

clue.text: Dig up half the estate? One's not getting involved with that

definitions.text: One's not getting involved with that

parts.note: to dig up a buried body is to disinter it

indicators.note: half means take the first three of the six letters of estate

explanation.surface: Someone wonders about excavating part of a property, then decides to stay out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the answer in a sentence: lack of involvement is what one has when staying out of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Disinterest properly means impartiality, having no stake, so it is a detached stance.

clue.text: … silence before old McCartney group's brief performance

parts.note: sh is a call for silence

indicators.note: brief means the group's name is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: Wings was Paul McCartney's band after the Beatles

explanation.surface: A hush falls before a short set by Paul McCartney's old band.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue 16 runs on into this one with an ellipsis; 'brief' cuts WINGS to WING.
explanation.definitionFit: A showing is a screening or exhibition, the presentation of a film or play.

clue.text: Remote area in France

indicators.note: in means the letter for area sits inside the abbreviation for France

explanation.surface: Someone mentions a remote region in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts A inside FR.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote places are distant, a long way off.

clue.text: Player, idle sort, grabbed by ref roughly

indicators.note: grabbed by means the idle letters are held inside the referee's letters
roughly means the letters of ref are rearranged
sort means the letters of idle are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A lazy player is grabbed roughly by the referee.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams: 'sort' rearranges idle and 'roughly' rearranges ref; 'grabbed by' puts the first inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket or baseball a fielder is a team member on the fielding side.

clue.text: Trailer for movie's early sequence

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: early sequence means the opening couple of letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A preview shows the opening scenes of a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'early sequence' gives MO, the opening two letters of movie.
explanation.definitionFit: A promo is a short promotional clip, which is what a film trailer is.

clue.text: Ally to elected US politician

parts.note: a pal is a friend or ally
a candidate who is elected is in

explanation.surface: Someone becomes an ally of an elected American politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Palin was Governor of Alaska and the 2008 Republican vice-presidential candidate.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarah Palin is a Republican who was Alaska's governor.

clue.text: Club managed by revolutionary sort in fashion

indicators.note: in means the words for managed and revolutionary go inside the word for fashion

parts.note: ton is an old word for fashion or style
to manage a business is to run it
Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary

explanation.surface: A club is run by a stylish revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like a society to be managed, but it is the weapon; TON is a dated word for high fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: A truncheon is a police baton, a short heavy stick used as a weapon.

clue.text: In this, one may be flung out of car hitting tree

definitions.text: In this, one may be flung out of car hitting tree

indicators.note: flung out of means the letter is thrown from the vehicle's word

parts.note: taken as written
A is one, the indefinite article
the ash is a tree

explanation.surface: A passenger is thrown out when a car hits a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be flung out of' throws the letter for one out of car; the tree follows. Read whole, the clue also describes the accident itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A road accident where a vehicle collides with something is a smash.

clue.text: Animal shelter maybe part of Blair agenda

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A refuge for animals might be one item on Tony Blair's programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was British Prime Minister 1997 to 2007.
explanation.definitionFit: A lairage is a pen where livestock are kept on the way to market or slaughter, a kind of animal accommodation.

clue.text: Observer newspaper, audio version

indicators.note: audio version means the word for the newspaper is heard, not read

parts.note: the i is a British daily newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone mentions the audio edition of the Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is a British Sunday paper, but here 'Observer' is the definition; the i is another British daily.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye is the organ that sees, so it watches like an onlooker.

clue.text: Temperature divine in most of the country? Poppycock

indicators.note: in means the divine's letters sit inside the shortened country
most of means drop the last letter of the country

parts.note: Wales is the country, part of the United Kingdom
DD, Doctor of Divinity, stands for a clergyman or divine

explanation.surface: A clergyman's temperature in much of the nation is called nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divine' looks like an adjective but is a clergyman, DD; 'most of' cuts WALES to WALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle is silly talk, rubbish or nonsense.

clue.text: What's on after the watershed gets you exploding with anger

indicators.note: exploding means the letters of the two words are blown apart and rearranged

explanation.surface: TV shown after the 9pm watershed makes a viewer furious.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the watershed is 9pm, after which adult TV may be shown; here 'What's on' means what you are wearing at bedtime.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyjamas and nightdresses are what people have on after bedtime, a joke on TV listings.

clue.text: YBA's success impresses Royal Society

definitions.note: YBA, one of the Young British Artists of the 1990s; the 's is a link

indicators.note: impresses means the word for success presses around the abbreviation

parts.note: a hit is a success
RS is the abbreviation for the Royal Society, Britain's science academy

explanation.surface: A young British artist's hit show impresses the scientific establishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The YBAs were the Young British Artists who rose in the 1990s, Damien Hirst the best known.
explanation.definitionFit: Damien Hirst, famous for a shark in formaldehyde, led the Young British Artists group.
